query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy nanoalloys that exhibit larger lattice distortions from diverse atomic sizes achieve superior structural and chemical stability at high temperatures because the severe lattice distortion induces sluggish atomic diffusion. This kinetic hindrance delays grain growth, phase separation, and deleterious oxidation by suppressing rapid chemical segregation and diffusion‐mediated reactions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, nanoscale high-entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory BCC or FCC alloy with equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition) synthesized via powder metallurgy or additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Slightly modify the alloy composition to vary the atomic size mismatch (and hence the lattice distortion) while keeping the overall phase structure similar. Expose samples to controlled high-temperature treatments (e.g., 800–1100 °C) in oxidizing environments.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air (or controlled oxidizing atmosphere) for extended durations (tens to hundreds of hours) to capture both short-term and long-term evolution of microstructure and surface oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion-induced sluggish diffusion which mediates the uniformity of the phase and retards chemical segregation and oxide growth.
generation.mechanism: The severe lattice distortion in high-entropy nanoalloys leads to lower diffusion coefficients at high temperatures. This sluggish diffusion retards the ability of atoms to rearrange into deleterious clusters or precipitates and slows the progression of oxidation by impeding the rapid transport of oxidizable species, thereby preserving both the microstructural homogeneity and chemical composition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys engineered to have higher lattice distortion (greater atomic size mismatch) will display reduced grain growth, lower rates of phase separation (or precipitation), and slower oxidation kinetics (e.g., lower weight gain or thinner oxide layers) compared to baseline alloys with lower lattice distortion.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy nanoalloy with a composition yielding moderate lattice distortion, processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold for the selected high-temperature range (roughly 800–1100 °C) and for nanoalloys where the phase remains a single-phase solid solution; at temperatures above this range or if the alloy decomposes into multiple phases, additional mechanisms (e.g., dynamic recrystallization) may become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: While the sluggish diffusion mechanism is supported by theoretical expectations in high-entropy systems, the precise interplay between protective surface oxide formation and diffusion-controlled processes is complex and may vary with alloy system and external environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of high-entropy nanoalloy samples with nearly identical compositions except that one series is doped with additional minor elements (chosen to increase atomic size mismatch and thus lattice distortion) while the other serves as the baseline with lower lattice distortion. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation treatments (e.g., 900 °C in air) for a fixed duration. Use electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to evaluate grain growth, phase stability, and oxide layer thickness/weight gain.
measurements: Grain size distribution via electron microscopy
Phase composition and any emergent precipitates via XRD
Oxidation kinetics measured by weight gain/TGA
Elemental mapping (e.g., by EDS) to assess chemical segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped (high lattice distortion) samples do not exhibit significantly reduced grain growth, phase separation, or slower oxidation kinetics (with statistically significant differences, p < 0.05) compared to the baseline samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion-induced sluggish diffusion governs the high-temperature stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system.
